topics.title: Introduction to The Incident of the Tooth
topics.summary: An introduction to the story adapted from Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, highlighting the themes of childhood mischief and school avoidance.
learning_objectives: Understand the context of the story

subtopics.title: Background and Context
subtopics.summary: Historical and literary context of the story.
subtopics.content: This story is based on an extract from the book, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, set in the fictional town of St Petersberg in nineteenth century America. Tom is an orphan who lives with his Aunt Polly, his half-brother, Sid and his cousin Mary.

topics.title: The Morning Misery
topics.summary: Tom Sawyer's reluctance to go to school on a Monday morning leads him to search for a reason to stay home.
learning_objectives: Understand the cause and effect of Tom's actions

subtopics.title: Tom's Dilemma
subtopics.content: Monday morning found Tom Sawyer miserable. Monday morning always found him so - because it began another week's slow suffering in school. I wish there were no holidays in between ... it just makes going back to school so much more difficult.

subtopics.title: Seeking Illness
subtopics.summary: Tom contemplates his physical state to skip school.
subtopics.content: Tom lay thinking. It occurred to him that he wished he were sick; then he could stay home. Hmm, am I ill? Is something wrong with me? Yes, I think my stomach is aching ... yes, it is certainly getting more painful!

topics.title: The Search for Symptoms
topics.summary: Tom experiments with different potential ailments to convince Aunt Polly he is sick.
learning_objectives: Examine the development of the plot

subtopics.title: The Tooth and the Toe
subtopics.summary: Tom finds a loose tooth but decides to keep it as a backup.
subtopics.content: Then he remembered hearing the doctor speaking about a certain illness that laid up a patient for two or three weeks. One could even lose a finger from it. I do have a sore toe. But if Aunt Polly comes to know about the tooth, she will want to pull it out, and that will hurt a lot. Tom decided to hold the tooth in reserve for the present and seek further.

subtopics.title: The Act of Groaning
subtopics.summary: Tom tries to get Sid's attention through performative groaning.
subtopics.content: Tom began groaning with spirit, but Sid slept on unconscious. Tom groaned louder and fancied that he began to feel pain in the toe. Tom was panting with his exertions by this time. He rested a moment and then swelled himself up and fetched a succession of admirable groans.

topics.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
topics.summary: Word meanings and glossary provided in the text.

subtopics.title: Glossary List
subtopics.summary: Key word meanings from the chapter.
subtopics.content: colicky: associated with a stomach ache. sore: painful and often, red. feeble: weak. fancied: imagined. reflected: thought. exertions: great efforts that make someone tired. hold in reserve: keep something available for later use. succession: (here) series.

topics.title: Interaction with Sid
topics.summary: Tom's attempts to wake Sid to witness his 'suffering'.

subtopics.title: Sid's Awakening
subtopics.summary: Sid wakes up and reacts to Tom's display.
subtopics.content: Tom was annoyed now. He called Sid loudly and shook him. What is the matter, Tom? Why, what's the matter, Tom? I must call auntie. Don't stir so, Sid, you'll kill me. OHHHHH!

topics.title: The Climax and Exposure
topics.summary: The resolution of Tom's trickery when Aunt Polly enters.
learning_objectives: Identify the climax of the story
Analyze the outcome of Tom's lies

subtopics.title: The Dying Act
subtopics.summary: Tom tries to make his sickness look fatal.
subtopics.content: I forgive everybody, Sid. Uhhhh! Tell 'em so, Sid. And Sid, you give my window sash and my cat with one eye to that new girl that's come to town, and tell her – Oh, Tom, you ain't dying, are you?

subtopics.title: Aunt Polly's Intervention
subtopics.summary: Aunt Polly discovers Tom is not really dying.
subtopics.content: Dying! Rubbage! I don't believe it! You, Tom! Tom, what's the matter with you? Oh, auntie, my sore toe's mortified! She laughed a little, then cried a little, then did both together. This restored her somewhat. Tom, what a turn you did give me. Your tooth, indeed! Now you shut up that nonsense and climb out of this.
learning_objectives: Understand the conclusion of the trick

topics.title: Grammar and Language Study
topics.summary: Focused sections on nouns, pronouns, and abstract concepts.
learning_objectives: Master personal, possessive, and reflexive pronouns

subtopics.title: Abstract Nouns
subtopics.summary: Definitions and formation of abstract nouns.
subtopics.content: Abstract nouns refer to things which we cannot see or touch but only feel. They include feelings, experiences, states, qualities and ideas. Example: Tom was suffering in reality now, so handsomely was his imagination working. Abstract nouns can be formed from verbs or adjectives. Examples: behave -> behaviour, speak -> speech, happy -> happiness. They are often formed by adding a suffix to the verb or adjective. Examples: silly -> silliness, communicate -> communication.

subtopics.title: Noun Exercises
subtopics.content: 1. The scientist's work led to an important discovered. 2. I have the greatest admiration for those who help animals. 3. The doctor prescribed three types of medicines for her ill. 4. I share all my happiness, both happy and sad, with my best friend. 5. The loudspeakers are causing annoyance to everyone in the area. 6. We found the house without any difficulty because of the host's clear directions.

subtopics.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
subtopics.summary: Distinguishing between countable and uncountable nouns.
subtopics.content: Read this sentence: Mary, get me some silk threads, and a chunk of fire out of the kitchen. Here, the noun threads is countable. You know that countable nouns can be singular or plural. The word fire is an uncountable noun. Language Booster: Not all nouns that end with s are plural countable nouns. Examples: measles, mathematics, billiards.
learning_objectives: Differentiate between countable and uncountable nouns

subtopics.title: Types of Pronouns
subtopics.content: Personal pronouns are used in place of the names of people and things. These are I, we, you, he, she, it, they, me, us, him, her and them. Example: It occurred to him that he wished he were sick. Possessive pronouns are used to show ownership and belonging. They are mine, yours, his, hers, ours, its and theirs. Example: The one-eyed cat is his. Reflexive pronouns are used when we want to refer back to the subject of the sentence. They are myself, yourself, himself, herself, oneself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, and themselves. Example: He swelled himself up and fetched a succession of admirable groans.

topics.title: Idioms and Figurative Language
topics.summary: Exploring idioms used in the chapter and common English expressions.
learning_objectives: Understand the meaning of idiomatic expressions

subtopics.title: Idiom Practice
subtopics.content: 1. spill the beans - e. tell a secret. 2. turn over a new leaf - a. change one's way of life to become a better, more responsible person. 3. cost an arm and a leg - d. very expensive. 4. the best of both worlds - c. receiving the benefits of two completely different situations at the same time. 5. not see eye to eye - b. not share the same views as somebody about something.
